query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating enhanced free energy sampling methods (e.g., metadynamics or umbrella sampling) with machine-learning optimized interatomic potentials will allow efficient and quantitatively accurate determination of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and key liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy (HEA) solid solutions covering a broad compositional space of multi-principal element systems.
generation.intervention: Implement an advanced simulation framework that couples enhanced free energy sampling techniques with ML-trained interatomic potentials.
generation.conditions: High-temperature regimes that span the solid-to-liquid transition and the liquid phase, applied across diverse HEA compositions representative of the full compositional diversity in the HEA family.
generation.structural_mediator: The computed free energy landscape capturing transient atomic rearrangements and nucleation events during melting, mediated by accurate interactions from ML potentials.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced free energy sampling (via metadynamics or umbrella sampling) efficiently overcomes the intrinsic free energy barriers of rapid phase transitions, while machine-learning optimized interatomic potentials ensure high energetic fidelity and computational speed. This combined approach accurately maps the melting process and liquid-state properties of complex alloy systems.
generation.predicted_outcome: The simulation framework will yield predictions for melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume change at melting, and other liquid-phase thermodynamic properties with errors within roughly 5% relative to high-precision experimental measurements. It is expected to achieve much greater efficiency than traditional calorimetric or CALPHAD-based methods.
generation.baseline: Traditional methods such as differential scanning calorimetry and CALPHAD calculations, which are typically either too time-consuming or insufficiently accurate across the wide compositional space of HEAs.
generation.boundary: The method may face limitations in alloys with extremely high melting points or highly refractory systems if sufficient ML training data is lacking, potentially requiring greater computational effort or encountering systematic deviations beyond the target error threshold.
generation.uncertainty: While early evidence supports the potential of enhanced sampling and ML potentials in capturing atomic-scale phase transitions, uncertainties remain regarding the scalability and universal accuracy of ML potentials across all HEA compositions, particularly for refractory alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of HEAs covering a wide compositional space. For each alloy, conduct simulations using the enhanced free energy and ML potential framework to predict melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and selected liquid-phase thermodynamic properties. Independently, obtain high-throughput, high-precision experimental measurements using methods such as in situ laser heating with synchrotron-based calorimetry on the same alloys.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation predictions for any of the key thermodynamic properties consistently deviate by more than approximately 5% from the experimental measurements in at least three distinct HEA compositions, the proposed approach would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. The LSF methodology proposed by Dong et al . [29] , [30] was adopted to describe the finite-temperature magnetic state of each alloy species in PM CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The root-mean-square magnetic moment m I ( w , T ) [30] , which is formulated as m I = ∫ μ 2 ⋅ x ( μ ) d μ with x ( μ ) being the spin-density distribution of longitudinal magnetic component μ , was used to represent the LSF energetics at thermal excitations in both the fcc and hcp phases. For the sake of computational feasibility of determining { m I }, we used the ‘fluctuating medium approximation’ and the ‘one shot from static equilibrium approach’ [29] . The present LSF methodology has been applied to PM bcc and fcc Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy, and the predicted finite-temperature properties such as single-crystal elastic constants [29] , [30] , lattice expansion [34] and intrinsic energy barriers [39] confirm the accurate description of the magnetic state at elevated temperatures.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are designed for high elevated-temperature strength, with both edge and screw dislocations playing an important role for plastic deformation. However, they can also display a significant energetic driving force for chemical short-range ordering (SRO). Here, we investigate mechanisms underlying the mobilities of screw and edge dislocations in the body-centered cubic MoNbTaW RHEA over a wide temperature range using extensive molecular dynamics simulations based on a highly-accurate machine-learning interatomic potential. Further, we specifically evaluate how these mechanisms are affected by the presence of SRO. The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced, although this influence of SRO appears to be attenuated at increasing temperature. Independent of the presence of SRO, a cross-slip locking mechanism is observed for the motion of screws, which provides for extra strengthening for refractory high-entropy alloy system.

decision.trend: In recent years, research on high‐entropy alloys has evolved from traditional experimental approaches—such as differential scanning calorimetry and annealing methods used in casting—to advanced processing techniques (e.g., selective laser melting, laser powder bed fusion, and high-pressure high-temperature treatments) that emphasize control over microstructure and phase formation. Although these studies have largely targeted mechanical properties and microstructural refinements in the high-temperature regime, they illustrate both the challenges of probing rapid phase transitions and the limitations of conventional calorimetric and CALPHAD-based methods when applied across the vast compositional span of HEAs.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in processing and mechanical performance characterization, no existing method has yet achieved both the high accuracy and the efficiency required to determine melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of HEAs. The challenge stems from the high computational cost of precise free energy calculations and the experimental difficulty of accessing fast phase-change dynamics over diverse compositions.
decision.lever: Develop and implement enhanced free energy calculation methods—such as metadynamics or umbrella sampling integrated with machine-learning optimized interatomic potentials—to accurately compute the melting free energy landscape
decision.why: Building on the trend of moving from traditional calorimetric and coarse computational methods toward advanced simulation techniques, this approach promises to deliver quantitative predictions (e.g., within 5% error) over a wide compositional space. Integrating enhanced sampling with ML potentials addresses the dual needs of efficiency and accuracy. A decisive validation would be a close match between these simulation-derived thermodynamic parameters and high-precision, high-throughput experimental measurements (for example, in situ laser heating or synchrotron-based calorimetry), with any systematic deviation ruling out the proposed approach.
